parsed_answer.content: WebClient is the non-blocking, reactive replacement for the legacy RestTemplate within the Spring ecosystem. While RestTemplate relies on a thread-per-request model—which inevitably leads to thread starvation under high concurrency—WebClient leverages the Project Reactor library to handle HTTP requests asynchronously. By utilizing an event-loop architecture, WebClient allows a small number of threads to manage thousands of concurrent connections, making it the cornerstone of high-performance microservices built on Spring WebFlux. It solves the 'blocking I/O' bottleneck by returning Mono or Flux types, effectively decoupling the request-response lifecycle from the underlying thread pool.

items: Event-Loop Efficiency: WebClient uses Netty as its default runtime, where a small fixed number of event-loop threads handle I/O events, preventing the overhead of context switching associated with large thread pools.
Reactive Streams Integration: Because it returns Mono<T> or Flux<T>, it integrates seamlessly with RSocket, Kafka, or other reactive data pipelines, allowing for end-to-end backpressure propagation.
Fluent API: The builder pattern allows for declarative configuration of headers, timeouts, and retry strategies, which are applied to the pipeline before the request is even subscribed to.
Cold vs Hot Streams: WebClient requests are 'cold' by default, meaning the HTTP call is only executed when a subscriber (like a controller or a flatMap) subscribes to the returned publisher.

parsed_answer.content: The most common production failure with WebClient is forgetting to subscribe or failing to handle the lifecycle of the reactive stream. If you call a WebClient method and do not return the Mono/Flux to the framework (e.g., Spring WebFlux controller), the request will never execute. Furthermore, avoid using .block() in production code; it forces the reactive pipeline to wait synchronously, effectively negating all the performance benefits of the non-blocking architecture and risking thread exhaustion.
